analogy.p: Think of f as a vending machine. You press a button (the input x) and out comes a product with a price (the output y). If a shop adds a flat 20p charge **after** the machine (f(x) + 0.2) every price rises by 20p: that is an **outside** change and the graph moves straight up. If instead someone changes the **button number** before it reaches the machine (f(x + 2)), then to get the same product you must press a button that is 2 lower, so the graph shifts left. Putting a minus in front of the price (−f(x)) turns every price upside down; putting a minus on the button (f(−x)) swaps left and right. The analogy breaks down because a real machine only has whole-number buttons, whereas a function accepts any number and its graph is a continuous curve.
analogy.t: The function machine and the vending machine

bullets: **y = f(x)** is the original graph; the changed graph is called the **image** and the original is the **object**.
Only **four** transformations are needed at Higher tier here: **f(x) + a** (up or down), **f(x + a)** (left or right), **−f(x)** (reflection in the x-axis) and **f(−x)** (reflection in the y-axis).

Every transformation moves **every** point of the graph by the same rule, so the **shape** is unchanged (it is congruent): the curve does not get wider, narrower or taller. (Stretches are not required for Edexcel 1MA1.)
Think about **key points**: turning points, x-intercepts (roots), y-intercept, and asymptotes. Move these first, then join them with the same shape.
The skill is split in two: **recognising** what a given equation does to a graph, and **describing** what has happened when you are shown an original and an image.
Questions often give a sketch of y = f(x) with labelled points and ask for the **coordinates** of the corresponding points on a transformed graph.
The notation f(x + 2) does **not** mean 'f times (x + 2)'; it means 'put x + 2 into the function f'.
core.p: A **function** is a rule that takes an input x and gives exactly one output, written **f(x)**. The graph **y = f(x)** is the set of all points (x, f(x)). A **transformation** changes the rule in a small, controlled way (adding a number, putting a minus sign in a particular place) and the whole graph is moved or flipped as a result. The Edexcel specification asks you to **sketch translations and reflections of a given function**, so you must be able to look at a graph (or a known shape such as a quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential or trigonometric curve), apply a change like f(x) + 3 or f(x − 2) or −f(x) or f(−x), and draw the new curve with its important points correctly placed.

bullets: Point rule: **(x, y) → (x, y + a)**.
y = f(x) + 3 is a translation by vector (0, 3); y = f(x) − 4 is a translation by vector (0, −4).
A turning point at (2, −5) on y = f(x) moves to (2, −2) on y = f(x) + 3.

The **y-intercept** moves by a (if f(0) = 4 then the new y-intercept is 4 + a), but the **roots (x-intercepts) usually change** because the curve now crosses the axis at different places, so you cannot work them out from the original without more information.
**Horizontal asymptotes** move too: y = 1/x has asymptote y = 0, but y = 1/x + 2 has asymptote y = 2 (see the figure).
For y = 2ˣ + 3 the asymptote is y = 3 and the y-intercept is 2⁰ + 3 = 4.
Exam check: after the transformation, **the same shape must appear**, just higher or lower; if your sketch has changed shape you have made a mistake.
core.p: When a number is added **outside** the function, it is added to every output (every y-value). So each point (x, y) becomes (x, y + a): the whole graph slides **up a units if a is positive** and **down a units if a is negative**. The x-coordinates do not change at all, which means the graph moves straight up or down without sliding sideways. This is the transformation that does exactly what it looks like: +3 on the end means 3 higher, −2 on the end means 2 lower. In vector language it is a **translation by the column vector (0, a)** (zero across, a up).

bullets: Point rule: **(x, y) → (x − a, y)** for y = f(x + a). The y-coordinate does not change.
y = f(x + 2): translation by vector **(−2, 0)**; y = f(x − 3): translation by vector **(3, 0)**.
Find the new position by asking: **what value of x makes the bracket equal to the old x-value?** For f(x − 3) the old point x = 0 now needs x − 3 = 0, so x = 3.
A turning point at (2, −5) on y = f(x) moves to (2 − 3, −5) = (−1, −5) on y = f(x + 3).
**x-intercepts** move by the same amount: if f crosses the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 5 then f(x + 3) crosses at x = −4 and x = 2.
The **y-intercept** is f(0 + a) = f(a), which is a different value; you cannot read it from the old graph unless the old graph shows f(a).
**Vertical asymptotes** move: y = 1/(x − 2) has asymptotes x = 2 and y = 0.
Check with a quadratic: y = (x − 3)² has its turning point when x − 3 = 0, so at (3, 0), which is 3 to the **right** of y = x².
core.p: When a number is added **inside** the brackets, it is added to the **input** before the function does its work. This changes the x-values, and it does so in the **opposite** direction to what most people expect. y = f(x + 2) is the graph of f **moved 2 units to the left**, and y = f(x − 3) is the graph of f **moved 3 units to the right**. The reason is that, for the new graph to give the same output as the old one, the new input must be smaller by 2: if f has its minimum at x = 0 then f(x + 2) has its minimum when x + 2 = 0, that is at x = −2. The vector for f(x + a) is **(−a, 0)**.

bullets: **Outside** the bracket (f(x) + a, −f(x)) affects the **y-values**: vertical changes.
**Inside** the bracket (f(x + a), f(−x)) affects the **x-values**: horizontal changes, and they work the **opposite** way to what the sign suggests.
Quick test: pick the key point, e.g. a minimum at x = 0 for y = x², and ask when the bracket equals zero. For (x + 2)² it is when x = −2, so the graph moved left.
Another test: substitute a number. If f(x) = x² then f(x − 3) at x = 3 gives f(0) = 0, the old minimum, so the minimum is now at x = 3.
A mark-scheme style phrase: 'translation by vector (−2, 0)' is worth more than 'it moves 2'.
The same reasoning gives **f(−x)**: negating the input reverses the x-direction, flipping the graph left to right.
core.h: Why inside and outside behave differently
core.p: It helps to picture f as a machine. A change **outside** the brackets happens **after** the machine has produced its output, so it acts directly on y and does what it says (y + 3 is 3 higher). A change **inside** the brackets happens **before** the machine, altering the input. To get the same result as before you must now feed in a number that is smaller or larger by the opposite amount, so the whole graph shifts in the opposite direction along the x-axis. Learning this reason is much more reliable than memorising 'left means plus'.

bullets: Point rule: **(x, y) → (x, −y)**.
Description for full marks: **'reflection in the x-axis'** (you must say 'reflection' and give the mirror line).
Roots (x-intercepts) are **invariant** (unchanged) because they lie on the mirror line.
The y-intercept changes sign: if f(0) = 3, then −f(0) = −3.
y = −x² + 4 is the reflection of y = x² − 4 in the x-axis, so a minimum at (0, −4) becomes a maximum at (0, 4).
Reflecting y = 2ˣ in the x-axis gives y = −2ˣ, which lies below the x-axis and still approaches y = 0 (the asymptote is unchanged because it is the mirror line).
For y = 1/x the branches move from quadrants 1 and 3 to quadrants 2 and 4: y = −1/x.
For y = sin x, y = −sin x is the same wave upside down, starting by going down, with the maximum at 270°.
core.p: A minus sign **outside** the function changes the sign of every output. A point (x, y) becomes (x, −y): positive y-values become negative and negative become positive. This flips the graph upside down in the **x-axis**, which acts as a mirror line. Points that are **on** the x-axis (the roots) have y = 0, and −0 = 0, so they do not move. Turning points swap type: a **minimum becomes a maximum** and a maximum becomes a minimum. This is the transformation that turns a smiley-shaped quadratic y = x² into the frowning y = −x².

bullets: Point rule: **(x, y) → (−x, y)**.
Description: **'reflection in the y-axis'**.
The **y-intercept** is invariant because it lies on the mirror line.
Example: f(x) = x² + 2x has roots 0 and −2; f(−x) = (−x)² + 2(−x) = x² − 2x has roots 0 and 2, and its turning point (1, −1) is the mirror image of (−1, −1).
y = 2⁻ˣ is the reflection of y = 2ˣ in the y-axis: exponential growth becomes exponential decay, still passing through (0, 1).
A turning point at (3, −4) becomes (−3, −4).
**Mistake to avoid:** f(−x) is not the same as −f(x). One flips left to right, the other flips top to bottom.
Extension: for an **odd function** (cubic y = x³, y = 1/x, y = sin x, y = tan x) f(−x) = −f(x), so both reflections give the same graph.
core.h: Reflection in the y-axis: y = f(−x)
core.p: A minus sign **inside** the brackets changes the sign of every input. A point (x, y) becomes (−x, y): the y-value stays the same, but the point swaps from one side of the y-axis to the mirror position on the other. The graph is therefore flipped left to right in the **y-axis**. Points on the y-axis (x = 0) do not move, so the **y-intercept is unchanged**. Roots change sign: if f has roots at x = 2 and x = −5, then f(−x) has roots at x = −2 and x = 5. For a graph that is already symmetrical about the y-axis, such as y = x² or y = cos x, reflecting in the y-axis gives exactly the same graph.

bullets: Example: a maximum at (4, 7). On y = f(x) − 2 it is (4, 5); on y = f(x + 1) it is (3, 7); on y = −f(x) it is (4, −7), now a minimum; on y = f(−x) it is (−4, 7).
Example: root at x = 6. On y = f(x − 2) it is x = 8; on y = f(−x) it is x = −6; on y = −f(x) it is still x = 6; on y = f(x) + 1 it is **not** known without more information.

**Asymptotes:** horizontal asymptote y = k moves with f(x) + a (to y = k + a) and flips with −f(x) (to y = −k); vertical asymptote x = h moves with f(x + a) (to x = h − a) and flips with f(−x) (to x = −h).
Write the new coordinates clearly in brackets: examiners need the form (x, y).
core.h: Moving key points: a rule table
core.p: Most exam questions give a sketch with some labelled coordinates and ask you to write down the corresponding coordinates after a transformation. The most reliable method is to apply the **rule for each change to every key point** and then redraw the curve through them. Always do this for turning points, because they determine where the curve sits. Use the table below, where (x, y) is a point on y = f(x) and the image is the point on the new graph.

bullets: **y = f(x + a) + b** is one translation by the vector **(−a, b)**.
Example: the graph of y = x² mapped to y = (x − 3)² + 1 is a translation by vector (3, 1); its turning point (0, 0) moves to (3, 1).
When describing a transformation, you must say **'translation'** and give the **vector** (not just 'move' or 'shift'), or say 'translated 3 to the right and 1 up'.
y = −f(x) + 3: apply − to every y first, then add 3. A point (x, y) → (x, 3 − y).
y = −f(x + 1): shift left 1 and flip in the x-axis (a point (x, y) → (x − 1, −y)).
y = f(−x) + 2: reflect in the y-axis then up 2: (x, y) → (−x, y + 2).
A **single transformation** question wants only one description: a vector, or a reflection with its mirror line.
Check by testing one easy point through the equation as well as through your geometric argument.
core.h: Combining transformations: translation vectors and order
core.p: Many questions use **two changes at once**, such as y = f(x + 2) − 3. A horizontal translation and a vertical translation are independent, so you can do them in either order: y = f(x + 2) − 3 is a single translation by the vector **(−2, −3)**, which means 2 left and 3 down. When a **reflection** and a translation are combined the order does matter and you follow the order the equation tells you: y = −f(x) + 3 means reflect in the x-axis, then move up 3; but y = −(f(x) + 3) = −f(x) − 3 means move up 3 first and then reflect, which ends up 3 below. Be careful and expand if in doubt.

bullets: y = (x + 3)² has turning point (−3, 0); y = (x − 3)² has turning point (3, 0).
y = x² − 5 has turning point (0, −5); y = x² + 4 has turning point (0, 4).
y = (x − 2)² + 7 has minimum point (2, 7) and line of symmetry x = 2.
y = −(x + 1)² + 6 has **maximum** point (−1, 6).
The sign in the bracket is the **opposite** of the x-coordinate of the turning point; the number outside is the y-coordinate **as written**.
Reflection in the y-axis of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y = (−x − 2)² + 1 = (x + 2)² + 1, with turning point (−2, 1).
The detailed method of completing the square is covered in the topic on turning points.
core.h: Quadratics: turning points in the form y = (x + p)² + q
core.p: The most common application is to the quadratic y = x², whose turning point is (0, 0). Replacing x with (x − p) translates it p units right, and adding q translates it q units up, so **y = (x − p)² + q has turning point (p, q)**. This is why completing the square is so useful: it writes any quadratic as a translation of y = x² and instantly gives the minimum or maximum point. A negative sign in front, y = −(x − p)² + q, reflects y = x² in the x-axis first, so the turning point (p, q) is now a **maximum**. The axis of symmetry is the vertical line **x = p**.

bullets: y = x³ + 2: cubic moved up 2, passes through (0, 2). y = (x − 1)³: moved right 1, passes through (1, 0).
y = −x³: reflection in the x-axis (and also in the y-axis, since the cubic is odd), falling from top left to bottom right.
y = 1/x + 2: asymptotes x = 0 and y = 2. y = 1/(x + 1): asymptotes x = −1 and y = 0.
y = −1/x: branches in quadrants 2 and 4.
y = 2ˣ + 3: asymptote y = 3, y-intercept 4. y = 2ˣ⁺¹ = 2 × 2ˣ passes through (0, 2).
y = −2ˣ: below the x-axis, passes through (0, −1), asymptote y = 0.
y = 2⁻ˣ: exponential decay, still through (0, 1).
On a sketch, draw asymptotes as **dashed lines** and label their equations.
core.h: Other standard graphs and their asymptotes
core.p: The same four changes apply to every graph you are expected to know, but you must remember the key features of each base graph. **Cubic** y = x³ passes through the origin and rotates through 180° about it (odd function). **Reciprocal** y = 1/x has two branches (quadrants 1 and 3) and asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0. **Exponential** y = kˣ (k > 0) passes through (0, 1), is always above the x-axis and has the horizontal asymptote y = 0. After a transformation, **translate the asymptotes as well as the points** and keep the curve approaching them without touching.

bullets: **y = sin x + 1**: maximum 2 at 90°, minimum 0 at 270°, passes through (0, 1).
**y = cos x − 2**: maximum −1 at 0° and 360°, minimum −3 at 180°, y-intercept (0, −1).
**y = sin(x + 90°)** is cos x (translation 90° left); **y = sin(x − 90°)** is −cos x (translation 90° right).
**y = cos(x − 90°)** is sin x.
**y = −sin x**: reflection in the x-axis; the first half-wave dips below the axis.
**y = cos(−x)** is the same as cos x, because cos is symmetrical about the y-axis (an even function); sin(−x) = −sin x.
For tan, translating horizontally moves the asymptotes with it; y = tan x + 1 moves every point up 1 but keeps the asymptotes at 90° and 270°.
Exact values often needed: sin 30° = 0.5, cos 60° = 0.5, tan 45° = 1, sin 90° = 1, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0.
core.p: For 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, **y = sin x** starts at (0, 0), rises to a maximum of 1 at 90°, crosses zero at 180°, reaches a minimum of −1 at 270° and returns to 0 at 360°. **y = cos x** starts at its maximum (0, 1), is 0 at 90°, has minimum −1 at 180°, is 0 at 270° and returns to 1 at 360°. **y = tan x** has period 180°, passes through (0, 0), (180°, 0) and (360°, 0) and has vertical asymptotes at x = 90° and x = 270°. Each transformation then applies: for example sin x + 1 moves the wave up by 1, sin(x − 90°) moves it 90° right, and the two graphs sin and cos are translations of each other.

bullets: **Step 1:** write down key points of the original: roots, y-intercept, turning points, asymptotes.
**Step 2:** apply the change to each: use (x, y + a), (x − a, y), (x, −y), (−x, y).
**Step 3:** plot the new points lightly, then draw one smooth curve (never a series of straight segments, never a flat bottom).
**Step 4:** label turning points and intercepts with coordinates, and draw dashed asymptotes with equations.
**Step 5:** check by testing one extra point (for example x = 0) in the new equation.
The sketch should **continue to the edges** of the axes shown with arrows or clearly extended curve ends.
Do not label roots that are not known: if the roots change in an unknown way (after f(x) + a), say so or sketch only what can be justified.
Take care that a minimum remains rounded (a U shape), not pointed.
core.h: Sketching a transformed graph: a step-by-step method
core.p: A **sketch** does not need accurate scales, but it must show the correct **shape**, the correct **position** and the **key points labelled** with coordinates. Use a repeatable method: first recognise the base shape and its key points, second apply the change to each key point using the rule table, third draw the new curve through these points with the same shape, and finally add labels, asymptotes and axis names. This gets the marks even when the drawing itself is not neat, because the mark scheme awards separate marks for shape, intercepts and turning points.

bullets: **Completing the square:** x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7 is y = x² translated by vector (−3, −7).
**Roots:** the roots of f(x + 2) are 2 less than the roots of f(x); the roots of f(−x) are the negatives.
**Solving f(x) = k:** the solutions are the x-coordinates where y = k meets y = f(x); translating the graph is equivalent to changing k.
**Geometry link:** a translation by (a, b) of any shape adds a to every x and b to every y; reflection in the x-axis negates y.
**Real life:** y = f(x) + a is a fixed-charge change (e.g. adding a call-out fee); f(x + a) is a time delay in a graph of distance against time.
**Trigonometry:** use y = sin(x + 90°) = cos x to link graphs.
**Higher tier:** be ready to identify a transformation from graphs given for a function on a coordinate grid with labelled points.
**Further:** transformations also include stretches y = af(x) and y = f(ax) at A-level, but these are not part of Edexcel GCSE 1MA1.
core.p: Graph transformations connect to many other areas. They explain **completing the square** (every quadratic is a translation of y = x²), they help with **solving equations graphically** (the solutions of f(x) = k are where the line y = k meets the graph), and they underpin **trigonometry** (cos is sin shifted) and **exponential growth and decay** (the asymptote shows the limiting value). They also connect to **transformations in geometry**, where translations use column vectors and reflections use mirror lines, so the same vocabulary and the same marks apply.

exam: **Typical marks:** write down new coordinates of a turning point = 1 mark; sketch a transformed curve = 2 to 3 marks (shape, turning point/intercept, asymptotes); describe a transformation fully = 2 marks (type + detail).

**Command words:** 'Write down' means no working (just the answer); 'Sketch' means a freehand graph with labelled key points; 'Describe fully' needs the name of the transformation AND the vector or mirror line; 'Show that' needs working to the stated result.
For a **translation**: say 'translation by the vector (a, b)' or 'translation 3 units to the right and 2 units up'. Writing 'move' or 'shift' alone usually earns 1 mark at best.
For a **reflection**: say 'reflection in the x-axis' or 'in the y-axis'; 'flip' is not accepted.
Do the new coordinates **point by point**: write (x, y) → (x − 3, y) beside each, then redraw the curve.
When y = f(x) is drawn on a grid, you are often asked to **plot** y = f(x) + 2 or similar on the same grid: translate 3 or 4 well-chosen points by the same amount and join with a smooth curve.
Label **asymptotes** with their equations (dashed lines) on sketches of y = 1/x + a, y = 1/(x − a) and y = kˣ + a.
For **trigonometric** sketches, mark maximum and minimum values on the y-axis and key angles (90, 180, 270, 360) on the x-axis.
Check with one value: substitute x = 0 into your new equation and make sure the y-intercept in your sketch matches.
**Beware of Algebra and Graphs links**: completing the square questions (e.g. 'write x² + 6x + 2 in the form (x + a)² + b, hence state the turning point') use the same ideas.

mistakes.r: f(x + 3) is a translation by vector (−3, 0): 3 units to the LEFT. A change inside the brackets works the opposite way.
mistakes.w: y = f(x + 3) moves the graph 3 to the right.

mistakes.r: f(x) + 3 is a translation by vector (0, 3): 3 units UP (a vertical change).
mistakes.w: y = f(x) + 3 moves the graph 3 to the right/left.

mistakes.r: y = −f(x) is a reflection in the x-axis; y = f(−x) is the reflection in the y-axis.
mistakes.w: y = −f(x) is a reflection in the y-axis.

mistakes.r: Say 'translation' and give the column vector (or both directions and distances) to earn both marks.
mistakes.w: Describing a translation as 'the graph moves 2 across' or 'shifts'.

mistakes.r: State 'reflection in the x-axis' or 'reflection in the y-axis' (or in the line x = a).
mistakes.w: Describing a reflection as 'flipped' without the mirror line.

mistakes.r: y = f(−x) changes only the sign of x: (3, −4) → (−3, −4). Only −f(x) changes the sign of y.
mistakes.w: Changing the signs of both coordinates for y = f(−x): (3, −4) → (−3, 4).

mistakes.r: Adding 2 outside moves the horizontal asymptote to y = 2; the vertical asymptote x = 0 stays.
mistakes.w: Moving the asymptote the wrong way (y = 1/x + 2 has asymptote x = 2).

mistakes.r: After a vertical translation the roots change. Roots only stay the same for −f(x), where they lie on the mirror line.
mistakes.w: Assuming roots stay the same after f(x) + a.

mistakes.r: Keep a smooth rounded U-shape (or ∩ for a maximum) through the correct turning point.
mistakes.w: Sketching a transformed parabola with a pointed or flat bottom.

summary: Edexcel Higher expects you to sketch and describe how the graph of y = f(x) changes under y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = −f(x) and y = f(−x), including where turning points, intercepts and asymptotes of standard graphs move to. It matters because it ties together quadratics, trigonometry, exponentials and geometry, and appears as 1 to 4 mark questions on Paper 2 and 3.

svg.cap: Horizontal translations: f(x + 2) is f(x) moved 2 to the LEFT, f(x − 3) is f(x) moved 3 to the RIGHT. Turning points sit at x = 0, −2 and 3.
Reflections of y = f(x) = x² + 2x. f(−x) is the mirror image in the y-axis (turning point (1, −1)); −f(x) is the mirror image in the x-axis (turning point (−1, 1)).
Transforming y = sin x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: sin x + 1 is the same wave shifted up 1; sin(x − 90°) is the same wave shifted 90° right, which is the graph of −cos x.
Asymptotes are translated with the curve. y = 1/x has asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0; y = 1/(x − 2) + 1 is the same shape moved 2 right and 1 up, so its asymptotes are x = 2 and y = 1 (dashed).
Summary of the four graph transformations required for Edexcel Higher.

terms.d: A rule that gives exactly one output for each input, written f(x).
A change to a graph or shape that alters its position or orientation (here translations and reflections).
A transformation that moves every point of a graph the same distance in the same direction; described by a column vector.
A transformation that flips a graph in a mirror line, producing a mirror image.
The line in which a reflection takes place (here the x-axis or the y-axis).
A pair of numbers (a, b) giving the movement across (a) and up (b) in a translation.
The graph or point obtained after a transformation.
A point where a curve changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa: a maximum or a minimum.
A value of x for which f(x) = 0; where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
A point where a graph crosses an axis: the y-intercept is where x = 0.
A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never touches or crosses at large values.
A line that divides a graph into two identical mirror halves, such as x = 2 for y = (x − 2)² + 1.
A point that does not move under a transformation, for example any point on the mirror line.
A freehand graph showing the shape and key features (intercepts, turning points, asymptotes) without needing accurate plotting.
A function with f(−x) = f(x); its graph is symmetrical about the y-axis (e.g. x², cos x).
A function with f(−x) = −f(x); its graph has 180° rotational symmetry about the origin (e.g. x³, sin x).

worked.q: The graph of y = f(x) has a minimum point at (2, −5) and crosses the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 5. Write down (a) the coordinates of the turning point on y = f(x) + 3, (b) the turning point on y = f(x + 3), (c) the turning point on y = −f(x), (d) the x-intercepts of y = f(−x). (4 marks)
steps: (c) −f(x): change the sign of y, so (2, −5) → (2, 5), and it is now a maximum (B1).
(d) f(−x): change the sign of every x: x = −1 → 1 and x = 5 → −5 (B1).

worked.ans: (a) y = −x² − 2x  (b) y = x² − 2x  (c) a translation by the vector (3, 1)
worked.q: The curve C has equation y = x² + 2x. (a) Write down the equation of the reflection of C in the x-axis. (b) Write down the equation of the reflection of C in the y-axis. (c) Describe fully the single transformation that maps y = x² onto y = (x − 3)² + 1. (5 marks)
steps: (b) y = f(−x) = (−x)² + 2(−x) = x² − 2x (B1). Check: C has roots 0 and −2, so the image has roots 0 and 2 (x² − 2x = x(x − 2)). ✓
(c) y = (x − 3)² is y = x² moved 3 to the right (inside bracket, opposite sign) (M1).
One translation: by the vector (3, 1). Check: the turning point (0, 0) moves to (3, 1). ✓ (A1)

worked.q: The graph of y = cos x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° is translated 2 units down. (a) Write down the equation of the new graph. (b) Write down the coordinates of the maximum and minimum points. (c) Write down the y-intercept. (d) Write down the equation of the graph of y = cos x after a translation of 90° to the right. (5 marks)
steps: (a) Subtract 2 outside the function: y = cos x − 2 (B1).
(b) cos x has maximum 1 at x = 0° and 360° and minimum −1 at x = 180°. Subtract 2: maxima (0°, −1) and (360°, −1), minimum (180°, −3) (B1 B1).
(d) Move right 90°: replace x with (x − 90°): y = cos(x − 90°) (B1). This is the same as y = sin x.
